notes.title: Start here: a help desk that shipped twenty backlog stories
notes.body:
This repo is the Agentic Help Desk: tickets, incidents, logs, background jobs and deterministic "agents" in one Next.js and Prisma monorepo. Its sibling quest covers the original agents, permissions and the first worker. This pack is about what came after: the twenty stories in `fabledocs/02-feature-backlog-user-stories.md`, all of which shipped.

Read in this order:

1. `fabledocs/01-how-this-app-works.md` sections 2, 4 and 6 (package layering, the seven-step server action, the worker loop).
2. The stories in epic C (SLA calendar, routing), epic D (job pipeline) and epics E and F (alert rules, knowledge base, the read-only API).

For each story, open the domain file it names under `packages/domain/src/` and compare the spec with the code. The spec was written first and the code sometimes chose differently (a dropped operator, a loop where a transaction was asked for). The quizzes key the code, so when the two disagree, believe the file.

excerpts.quote: Every story in document 02 was implemented on its own branch and merged through a reviewed pull request.
Where it disagrees with `docs/`, trust `fabledocs/`, and check the code itself if it matters.

notes.title: The job pipeline: claim, fail, back off, reclaim, requeue
notes.body:
Background jobs move through a small state machine owned by `packages/db/src/worker.ts` and the pure helpers in `packages/domain/src/jobs.ts`.

Four ideas to hold while reading:

- **Optimistic claim.** `claimNextJob` reads a candidate, then updates it only if its status (and `runAt`) still match. Losing the race is not an error.
- **Backoff.** After a failure the job is rescheduled by `nextRunAt`. Work out by hand how `calculateBackoffMs` combines the exponential base, the cap and the jitter, and check each step against the final `return`.
- **Leases.** A claim stamps `lockedAt`. `reclaimExpiredLeases` runs before every claim and returns abandoned work to the queue. Note which fields it writes and which it leaves alone.
- **Dead letters.** Once retries are exhausted, a human can review grouped failures on `/jobs/dead-letter` and requeue them with a reason.

When a function compares a time against a constant, write down whether the comparison is strict or inclusive, and compare it with how story D2 words that boundary.

notes.title: Rules, templates and keys: small engines with explicit edges
notes.body:
Several stories add a small engine with a pure evaluator and an explanation trail:

- `packages/domain/src/routing.ts`: ordered rules, every condition must hold, and an `evaluated` list explains each near miss. Compare the spec's operator list with `ROUTING_OPERATORS`, and read `conditionMatches` for how free-text fields are handled. Then find where `createTicketAction` calls the evaluator, and read the lines around the call.
- `packages/domain/src/canned-replies.ts`: the variable list is the security boundary. Read the placeholder regex and every branch of the replacer callback.
- `packages/domain/src/log-alerts.ts`: each early return carries its own reason. List the checks in order.
- `apps/web/lib/api-auth.ts` with `packages/domain/src/api-keys.ts`: how a key is found and compared, and which status each kind of failure returns.
- `packages/domain/src/business-hours.ts` and `calculateSlaDueAt`: business-hours arithmetic in UTC, and a rule about which priorities use it.

A good habit for each one: trace a concrete input through it on paper before reading the tests.

excerpts.quote: Evaluate rules in order and return the first match.
This list is the security boundary.

notes.title: Why the capped delay still carries its jitter
notes.body:
`calculateBackoffMs` caps the exponent at 20, so the base is `min(30,000 * 2^20, BACKOFF_MAX_MS)`, which is the one-hour cap. Jitter is `idJitter(jobId) * 8`, so a jitter value of 500 adds 4,000 ms. The last line is `min(base + jitter, BACKOFF_MAX_MS + jitter)`, and both sides are 3,604,000 ms.

- *3,600,000 ms* would be right only if the final clamp were against `BACKOFF_MAX_MS` alone; it adds the jitter to the cap too.
- *3,600,500 ms* forgets the multiplication by 8.
- *4,500,000 ms* invents a 25% jitter on the cap; the comment says up to about 25% of the **base** (30 s), not of the hour.

notes.title: Strict for leases, inclusive for heartbeats
notes.body:
`isLeaseExpired` returns `now - lockedAt > JOB_LEASE_MS`: at exactly five minutes the difference equals the lease, so it is **not** expired. `workerHealth` returns stale when `silentFor >= WORKER_STALE_MS`: at exactly 60 seconds the worker is **stale**. Story D2 says "over a minute" for stale, but the code makes the minute itself count.

- *Lease expired, worker stale*: wrong on the lease, which needs strictly more than five minutes.
- *Valid lease, healthy worker*: wrong on the heartbeat, which uses `>=`.
- *Both trip*: wrong on the lease, and a 60-second silence is stale, not dead (dead needs five minutes).

notes.title: What the lease reaper writes, and what it leaves
notes.body:
`reclaimExpiredLeases` is one `updateMany` over rows that are RUNNING with a `lockedAt` older than the lease. It writes `status: "RETRYING"`, `lockedAt: null` and `lockedBy: null`, and nothing else. The comment explains both choices: RETRYING tells "recovered after a worker died" apart from "never started", and `attempts` is left alone because the attempt really was made.

- *QUEUED with attempts reset* contradicts both halves of that comment.
- *FAILED with attempts raised* is the worker's catch block, which only runs when a job throws while a live worker holds it.
- *Left RUNNING* was the behaviour before story D2, the bug the reaper fixes.

excerpts.quote: untouched: the attempt was made, it just never reported back.

notes.title: A manual retry moves the clock, not the counter
notes.body:
`canRetryJob` allows FAILED **or** RETRYING while `attempts < maxAttempts`, so a RETRYING job at 2 of 3 is eligible. `retryJobAction` then sets `status: "RETRYING"` and `runAt: new Date()`, clearing the timestamps. It never writes `attempts`: since story D1 the worker is the only writer of that counter.

- *attempts becomes 3, runAt unchanged* describes the old double-counting behaviour, in reverse: the click used to burn an attempt.
- *It throws* is wrong because RETRYING is in the allowed list.
- *Dead-lettered at once* would need the action to raise attempts, which it does not.

excerpts.quote: This only makes the job due immediately, overriding any backoff delay.

notes.title: Requeue filters the batch instead of failing it
notes.body:
After the reason check (at least 10 characters), `requeueDeadLetterJobsAction` loads the selected jobs and keeps those that pass `canRequeueJob`: DEAD_LETTERED with `requeueCount < MAX_REQUEUES` (3). The three eligible jobs get `status: "QUEUED"`, `attempts: 0` and `runAt: now`; the two at the limit are counted and reported as `blocked=2` in the redirect.

- *All five* would need the reason to bypass `canRequeueJob`; it does not.
- *None* would need the action to throw on an ineligible job; it filters instead.
- *Attempts kept* is wrong: the code resets attempts so the backoff ladder starts fresh.

notes.title: Two failures, one readable group
notes.body:
`normalizeErrorMessage` lowercases the text, replaces runs of eight or more hex characters with `<id>`, then replaces digit runs with `<n>` and collapses spaces. Both messages become `timeout after <n>ms on hook <id>`, and `groupDeadLetters` keys on type plus that text, so there is one group with a count of 2.

- *Two groups because of case and ids*: case and ids are exactly what the normaliser removes.
- *Only with a shared requestContextId*: the group key has no request context in it.
- *Leaves ids and durations alone*: the comment says it applies the same idea as log fingerprints, just without hashing.

notes.title: Free-text fields always use a substring test
notes.body:
`conditionMatches` lowercases and trims both the condition value and the ticket value. For TITLE_CONTAINS and DESCRIPTION_CONTAINS it sets `substringField`, and `useContains` becomes true whatever the operator says. "cannot login after reset" includes "login", so the condition matches.

- *"equals" needs the whole title*: true for CATEGORY or TAG, not for these two fields.
- *The capital L blocks it*: `norm()` lowercases both sides.
- *The operator defaults to contains*: the schema default is "equals", and here the operator was set explicitly anyway.

notes.title: A human choice switches routing off entirely
notes.body:
`createTicketAction` evaluates routing rules only inside `if (!parsed.assignedTeamId && !parsed.assignedUserId)`. With Billing chosen, `routing` stays null, so `routedPriority` falls back to the submitted priority, `routedTags` is just the submitted tags, and the `matchCount` update (guarded by `routing?.matchedRuleId`) never runs.

- *Billing but HIGH and "sso"*: the rule's other effects are skipped along with its team, because the rule is never evaluated.
- *Platform and HIGH*: story C3 says an explicit choice overrides all routing, and the code agrees.
- *matchCount rises*: no rule matched, because none was evaluated.

notes.title: Unknown or unfilled placeholders stay visible
notes.body:
`PLACEHOLDER_PATTERN` is `\{\{\s*([a-zA-Z]+)\s*\}\}`, so `{{ ticketTitle }}` with spaces still matches and renders "SSO loop". The replacer returns the original text in two cases: the name is not in `CANNED_REPLY_VARIABLES` (priority), or the name is known but no value was supplied (agentName).

- *Blanks for the gaps* is what the comment rejects: a hole in a customer email nobody would notice.
- *Spaces stop ticketTitle matching*: the `\s*` in the pattern allows them.
- *An error*: unknown names are left as written, never thrown on or evaluated.

excerpts.quote: return value === undefined || value === null ? original : value;

notes.title: Authentication failures are 401, scope failures are 403
notes.body:
`authenticateApiRequest` looks the key up by prefix, compares hashes in constant time and checks `isApiKeyUsable`. A revoked key fails that combined check and gets the same 401 body as a missing or unknown key. A real, usable key without the scope gets 403, because the key is valid but not allowed.

- *Both 403*: the revoked key never reaches the scope check.
- *404 for the scope*: 404 is `notFoundResponse`, used for a record in another organization, not for scopes.
- *410 Gone*: the code deliberately gives revoked keys no distinct status.

excerpts.quote: 403 rather than 401: the key is real, it simply may not do this.

notes.title: Only DUPLICATE_OF has a reverse guard
notes.body:
`validateTicketLink` has three refusals: a self-link, an exact repeat (same source, target and type), and, for DUPLICATE_OF only, an existing DUPLICATE_OF in the opposite direction. B RELATED_TO A is not a self-link and not an exact repeat of A DUPLICATE_OF B, so it is ok. B DUPLICATE_OF A hits the reverse guard.

- *Both refused*: being linked one way does not block a different link type.
- *Both ok*: misses the reverse-duplicate rule.
- *RELATED_TO refused, reverse accepted*: the opposite of the code.

notes.title: HIGH walks the calendar; CRITICAL stays on the wall clock
notes.body:
With a calendar row present, `calculateSlaDueAt` uses `addBusinessHours` when `usesBusinessHours(priority)` is true, which is every priority except CRITICAL. HIGH needs 8 working hours: 1 on Friday (16:00 to 17:00), then 7 from Monday 09:00, ending at 16:00. CRITICAL adds 2 elapsed hours to Friday 16:00.

- *Saturday 00:00 for HIGH* is the elapsed-hours answer.
- *CRITICAL on Monday at 10:00* applies the calendar to CRITICAL, which the code forbids.
- *Monday 17:00 for HIGH* counts 8 hours from Monday and forgets Friday's last hour.

notes.title: The first failing check names the reason
notes.body:
`evaluateLogAlertRule` checks, in order: inactive, then `matchedCount < thresholdCount`, then the anomaly score, then cooldown. Three logs against a threshold of 5 fail at the second check, so the reason is "Only 3 matching log(s); threshold is 5." The result still reports `inCooldown: true`, because cooldown is computed up front.

- *Cites the cooldown*: cooldown is checked last on purpose, to mean "would have fired but recently did".
- *Fires on the score*: the count check runs before the score and is not outweighed by it.
- *Cites the score*: a score of 90 passes the minimum of 70 anyway.
